subject.title: RFC: Standard Hosting Profiles and Ready Check

question: Should OpenClaw core own named, release-tested hosting profiles, and which minimal readiness contract should be accepted first?
rationale: The RFC creates permanent public configuration, probe, status, support, and release-conformance obligations that implementation quality alone cannot authorize.

options.title: Accept readiness foundation
options.body: Approve the condition model and default local projection first, deferring each non-local profile and the blocking release gate to separately accepted, proven follow-ups.

options.title: Accept all four profiles
options.body: Sponsor the complete profile catalog and release gate after reviewing live fresh-install and upgrade evidence for every promised contract.

options.title: Keep checks host-owned
options.body: Decline core profile selection and continue exposing generic runtime facts for hosts and supervisors to validate downstream.

recommendation.title: Accept readiness foundation
recommendation.body: Approve the condition model and default local projection first, deferring each non-local profile and the blocking release gate to separately accepted, proven follow-ups.

likelyOwner.reason: He has the strongest direct history on the existing Gateway readiness endpoints whose compatibility semantics this RFC would extend.
